\chapter{El Mostrador --- Ticket, Coin, Passport, Entrance, Change}
\label{ch:el-mostrador}
\hlchaptermodality{313}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can get through a counter in Spanish: ask for the ticket, hand over the passport, find the entrance and ask for my change.}

Complete ES-C313-cambio: ask for a ticket, produce the passport, find the entrance and ask for the change owed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el boleto]{el boleto — a little seal, and what it authorises}

\label{lesson:ES-C313-boleto}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What was a \emph{mappa}? (A cloth.) And what is \emph{la carta}, on a table? (The menu — the sheet the dishes are on.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bo-LE-to}, stress on the middle. Every vowel is short and clean; none of them drift. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el boleto} — \textquotedblleft{}the ticket.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{bulla} started as a bubble or a round boss, and then became the thing that mattered: the \textbf{lead seal} hung on a document to prove it was genuine. The seal was the authority. The words were only what the seal was vouching for.

Italian made \emph{bulletta}, a little sealed slip, and Spanish took it as \emph{boleto}. A ticket is a small document with something official pressed into it. That is still exactly what it is.

English kept the seal in two places. A \textbf{bulletin} is a \emph{little bulla} — a short notice issued with authority. And a papal \textbf{bull} is named after the lead seal swinging from its ribbon, not after anything in the text.

One note on geography, since you will meet both. Spain mostly says \emph{billete}; most of Latin America says \emph{boleto}. They are the same \emph{bulla}, borrowed at different times down different roads. Either will be understood; \emph{boleto} is the one to carry across the Americas.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first word at the counter, and it is a seal rather than a slip of paper.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el boleto}
  \item \emph{el boleto, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — el boleto, por favor}
  \item \emph{el mapa}, then \emph{la carta}, then \emph{el boleto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{bulla}? (A lead seal on a document.) Why is a papal bull called that? (For its seal.) And what is \emph{la carta}? (The letter, or the menu.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la moneda]{la moneda — money is named after a goddess who gave warnings}

\label{lesson:ES-C313-moneda}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is \emph{la carta}? (The letter, or the menu.) And what was a \emph{bulla}? (A lead seal.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mo-NE-da}, stress on the middle. The \emph{d} between vowels is soft, the tongue barely touching. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la moneda} — \textquotedblleft{}the coin.\textquotedblright{}

This one is a place, and the place is named after a goddess.

Latin \emph{monere} meant \textbf{to warn}. One of Juno's titles was \textbf{Moneta}, \textquotedblleft{}she who warns\textquotedblright{} — the story is that her sacred geese warned Rome of an attack in the night. Rome built her a temple on the Capitoline hill, and in that temple, for reasons of security rather than religion, the city set up its coin works.

So the coins came out of the \emph{Moneta}. And the name of the building became the name of what the building produced.

English got it twice again, by the two familiar roads. Through French, worn down: \textbf{money}. Through Germanic mouths, worn differently: \textbf{mint}, the place coins are struck. Money and a mint are one goddess.

Her verb is still in English too, unchanged in sense. A \textbf{monitor} warns you. To \textbf{admonish} is to warn somebody toward something. A \textbf{monument} is a warning left standing so nobody forgets.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A ticket and a coin: the two things that cross a counter in opposite directions.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la moneda}
  \item \emph{una moneda, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — una moneda, por favor}
  \item \emph{la carta}, then \emph{el boleto}, then \emph{la moneda}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{monere} mean? (To warn.) Which two English words are both \emph{moneta}? (\emph{Money} and \emph{mint}.) And what is \emph{el boleto}? (The ticket.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pasaporte]{el pasaporte — a word that is its own instructions}

\label{lesson:ES-C313-pasaporte}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What was a \emph{bulla}? (A lead seal.) And which two English words are the goddess \emph{Moneta}? (\emph{Money} and \emph{mint}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-sa-POR-te}, stress on the third of four. Every \emph{s} stays clear and hissed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pasaporte} — \textquotedblleft{}the passport.\textquotedblright{}

Two pieces, both of which you can see without help. \emph{Pasar}, \textbf{to pass}, and \emph{porte}, from Latin \textbf{porta}, a \textbf{gate}. A passport is the paper that lets you \textbf{pass the gate}. It was originally permission to leave through a city's walls, not permission to enter a country.

\emph{Passus} was a \textbf{step} in Latin — the pace of a marching legion, and the unit Roman roads were measured in. English keeps the step in \textbf{pace}, in \textbf{pass}, and in a \textbf{passage}, which is the place stepping happens.

\emph{Porta} you have met before, standing in the harbour. A \textbf{port} is a gate for ships. A \textbf{portal} is a grand one. A \textbf{porch} is the little roofed gate of a house, and a \textbf{portico} its columned cousin.

Put the two back together and the word tells you its own job: step, gate, permission. Very few words are this honest.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ticket, coin, passport. The counter is nearly complete.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pasaporte}
  \item \emph{el pasaporte, por favor}
  \item \emph{un momento — el pasaporte}
  \item \emph{el boleto}, then \emph{la moneda}, then \emph{el pasaporte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Take \emph{pasaporte} apart. (Pass, plus gate.) What was a \emph{passus}? (A step.) And what is \emph{la moneda}? (The coin.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la entrada]{la entrada — the way in, and the paper that buys it}

\label{lesson:ES-C313-entrada}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. Which two English words are the goddess \emph{Moneta}? (\emph{Money} and \emph{mint}.) And what does \emph{pasaporte} say it does? (Lets you pass the gate.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en-TRA-da}, stress on the middle. The \emph{r} in \emph{tra} is a single tap, quick and light. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la entrada} — \textquotedblleft{}the entrance,\textquotedblright{} and also the ticket that gets you in.

Latin \textbf{intrare}, to go in, was built on \emph{intra}, \textbf{within}. Everything here is the idea of being inside a boundary rather than outside it.

English took the verb through French and softened it: \textbf{enter}. The noun kept more of the shape — an \textbf{entrance}, an \textbf{entry}. And the raw Latin \emph{intra-} stayed raw wherever precision mattered: \textbf{intramural} means within the walls, \textbf{intravenous} within the vein, \textbf{interior} the inside itself.

Spanish does something neat with \emph{entrada} that English splits into two words. The place you go in is \emph{la entrada}. The ticket that permits it is also \emph{la entrada}. One word for the door and the right to use the door, which saves you learning a second.

Notice how it sits beside the last two. \emph{El boleto} rides you somewhere. \emph{La entrada} lets you in. \emph{El pasaporte} gets you past a border. Three permissions, three different edges.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four at the counter, and three of them are permissions rather than objects.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la entrada}
  \item \emph{una entrada, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe, ¿dónde está la entrada?}
  \item \emph{la moneda}, then \emph{el pasaporte}, then \emph{la entrada}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{intra} mean? (Within.) What does \emph{intramural} mean, literally? (Within the walls.) And what is \emph{el pasaporte} made of, in two pieces? (Pass, and gate.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cambio]{el cambio — a Gaulish word that outlived Gaulish}

\label{lesson:ES-C313-cambio}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What does \emph{pasaporte} say it does? (Lets you pass the gate.) And what does \emph{la entrada} name, besides the door? (The ticket that lets you through it.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CAM-bio}, stress on the first part. The \emph{-bio} ending is one glide, and the \emph{b} after \emph{m} closes the lips fully. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cambio} — \textquotedblleft{}the change.\textquotedblright{}

Late Latin had the verb \textbf{cambiare}, to exchange one thing for another. But Latin did not build it. Latin \textbf{borrowed} it, from Gaulish — the Celtic language spoken across what is now France before the legions arrived.

That is worth sitting with. Gaulish died, and what survives of it is a handful of inscriptions. Yet Rome took this one verb, and Rome's daughters carried it everywhere: Spanish \emph{cambiar}, French \emph{changer}, Italian \emph{cambiare}. English took the French form and made \textbf{change} of it, then \textbf{exchange} and \textbf{changeling}.

Every time an English speaker says \emph{change}, a dead language is being spoken.

Spanish uses \emph{el cambio} for the act and for the result: the rate at a bank window, and the coins pressed back into your hand at a till.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twenty words across four runs, and every one is something a stranger is holding.

The repairs kept an exchange alive; these give it something to be about. A noun after \emph{por favor} is a request in Spanish, and that is what this node is for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cambio}
  \item \emph{¿y el cambio?}
  \item \emph{disculpe — el cambio, por favor}
  \item \emph{el pasaporte}, then \emph{la entrada}, then \emph{el cambio}
  \item \emph{gracias}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which dead language gave Latin \emph{cambiare}? (Gaulish.) What two things does \emph{el cambio} name? (The exchange, and the coins handed back.) And what is \emph{la entrada}? (The entrance, or the ticket in.)
\end{tcolorbox}
